diagnosis.what_is_wrong: No kernel-level impairment is established, so the report that the coding task ran long cannot be confirmed as a host fault from this trace. A distinct activity burst occurs when `python3` and `http` become active, but the four-CPU host retains substantial idle capacity and runnable tasks are dispatched promptly; the burst is better explained as a workload phase change than resource saturation.
diagnosis.evidence: The full trace spans 18:58:32.300–18:58:51.400. Whole-span event-rate comparisons show a synchronized rise around 18:58:43 and fall around 18:58:50, while process-lifetime/runtime evidence attributes much of the burst to `python3` and `http` in pid_ns 4026531836. Compared with the preceding 18:58:36–18:58:43 range, scheduler runtime during 18:58:43–18:58:50 used only 6.264 CPU-seconds over seven seconds on four CPUs (22.4% capacity; no 100-ms bucket above 41%, versus 25.1% in baseline). Raw scheduler pairing within 1 ms on any CPU gave 47 burst wake-to-dispatch matches with p95 16.9 µs and max 21.9 µs; the 40 matched `http` samples had p95 6.8 µs. Disk request issue rates were broadly similar (about 261/s before versus 291/s during); the limited matched request sample had p95 2.83 ms during the candidate burst. Sampled network transmissions succeeded (rc=0), and dirty memory was well below the recorded thresholds. The falsification check for CPU starvation/saturation was run using runtime accounting and raw wake/switch records and did not support it; disk and network mechanism checks also did not show a fault signature. `ctf_lines` access failed according to the notes, so raw fields were inspected through indexed `get_lines` instead. Kernel evidence cannot establish the coding task's end-to-end duration, and there are no application-level measurements in this dataset.
diagnosis.window_evidence: The activity change has measurable boundaries at about 18:58:43 (rates rise and `http` appears) and 18:58:50 (rates collapse), but checks of CPU capacity, dispatch delay, disk, and sampled network records do not establish an impairment during that interval. Therefore it is an observed workload-burst window, not a supported incident window.
